It’s our job to protect Americans while also advancing innovation. That’s why I'm joining @JayObernolte, @RepGuthrie, & @RepMMM to request additional information from the @FDA on policies to leverage health AI for patients.

Read the letter: https://t.co/iwry7wjfu1

President Trump’s celebration of the Right to Try Act in his nomination speech is a better roadmap for health care policy.

We should prioritize treatment for vulnerable Americans. This law provides federal protections so that certain unapproved drugs with potential lifesaving benefits can be administered to desperate terminally ill patients who have exhausted all FDA approved treatments. 

Discovering new breakthroughs requires balancing risk and innovation. It’s critical that future public policy ensures greater access to personalized medicine that doesn’t neatly fit current regulatory boxes. 

President Trump is already setting the right tone to secure America’s dominance in medical innovation. Under his leadership, the new policies I support—such as pathways for regenerative medicine, preventing government over-regulation of medical AI, and coverage policies for products that address unmet needs like PTSD and rare disease—will have a better chance of success.

Onward.

We’ll cover a wide range of topics—everything from immigration to artificial intelligence, energy security, media and politics, diplomatic affairs, cartels, health care, and more. You’ll  learn how our government really works, and why it was created this way in the first place.

Congressman, as a member of the military and the Securities and Exchange Commission, I think we need to look holistically at AI across the board and not look at it just necessarily in the isolated world of financial background or the military side. [...] but also learn where we need to put holistic protections in place and how we can sort of learn from it and adopt appropriately.
statements.context: Verbatim remarks during a congressional oversight hearing on the Securities and Exchange Commission.

If we continue to standby while watching the world around us adapt to the next frontier of threats then we’re setting ourselves up for a catastrophic failure. 
 
The reality is, we approach this problem the wrong way. People think about it as a Russia-Ukraine style drone mobilization led by warfighters but some teenager in his room with access to ChatGPT could carry something like this out NOW. 
 
The threat’s already here, it’s not hypothetical. We need to arm our critical infrastructure to defend itself.
 
From the latest episode of Hold These Truths with defense expert Dr. Seth Jones.

The first battle in the War on Terror was on Flight 93, when forty Americans made the decision to fight back against evil. Today I visited the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, PA.

It’s an incredible place, and reminds us how quickly ordinary people can become heroes. From the moment they were hijacked to the moment they fought back was only 29 minutes. These brave Americans made the decision to fight for their lives in only 29 minutes.

Twenty-five years later, the threats to our homeland look different—cyberattacks, drones, AI, foreign espionage, and adversaries exploiting gaps in our security.

We cannot wait for another catastrophe to remind us what complacency costs. We have to recognize these threats and act before Americans pay the price again.

statements.quoted:
Made Grok and Claude hash out the exit poll data to get a more complete picture of voter sentiment.  Notably, they concluded Iran was an accelerant on issues, but not actually the top issue.  Their concurrent conclusions actually mirror a lot of public opinion polling that was showing up in the weeks before the election.

1Cost of living and inflation. 79% say inflation caused their family severe or moderate hardship. 62% blame higher prices more on Trump's policies than on factors beyond his control. 65% say his policies worsened the economy, against 27% who say they improved it. 75% rate the economy poor, 44% say they are worse off than two years ago, and 39% named the economy the top issue. BBC · AP via PBS · NBC

2Tariffs. 64% say tariffs hurt the national economy (D 78–19), and 63% say they hurt their local economy (D 79–18). Only 15% say tariffs helped their area. That is the most lopsided policy verdict in the poll, and voters judged it by their own towns. NBC

3Government corruption. 90% called it a crucial or major factor. About half called it "crucial," a larger share than for immigration, Iran, or AI, and about 6 in 10 say Trump puts his own interests first. About 4 in 10 voters who called it crucial still went Republican. BBC

4The Iran war and fuel costs. 63% say the attack was the wrong decision, against 37% who say it was right. 74% called the war a crucial or major factor, though only about a third called it crucial. 59% are "very concerned" about gas and diesel prices. Gas averaged $4.15, about $1.11 above a year earlier, and diesel averaged $6.29. About a quarter of Republicans say the war was wrong. BBC

5Democracy and checks on Trump. 32% named the state of democracy the top issue, and about 8 in 10 of them voted Democratic. About 7 in 10 say Congress isn't checking the President enough, including about 4 in 10 Republicans. 43% voted to oppose Trump and 16% to support him. His approval stood at 38%. BBC

6Immigration (the GOP's floor). 14% named it the top issue. Republicans kept a small edge on the issue, and it mattered more to Republican voters. Even so, 57% say enforcement has gone too far. BBC

7Healthcare. Democrats held a wide advantage here, but few voters named it the top issue.

8AI and data centers. It ranked below corruption and cost of living, and voters split on which party handles AI better. 61% opposed new data centers near them.

Context: 38% of voters were angry and 37% dissatisfied. By group:
•Women went D 58–40.
•Voters under 45 went roughly two-thirds D.
•Hispanic voters went D 62–35.
•College graduates went D 62–36.
•Non-college voters went R only 51–47.
•White voters went R only 51–48.

Just under half view Democrats favorably, against about 4 in 10 for the GOP.
